clue.text: Churned out in the land of cakes? That's for suckers

blocks.note: butter is what comes out of a churn
Scotland is nicknamed the land of cakes (oatcakes), so its produce is Scotch

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark about Scottish dairy produce, dismissed as something only fools would fall for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suckers' looks like dupes, but it means people sucking sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterscotch is a hard toffee sweet, made to be sucked slowly.

clue.text: Company over water abroad controlling locks

indicators.note: in a down clue, one part placed over another comes first in the column

blocks.note: a band is a company of people
the French word for water

explanation.surface: A firm runs canal water overseas, managing the locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' are hair, not canal gates.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandeau is a narrow headband that holds hair in place.

clue.text: Horse on canal path being one of strength?

blocks.note: first meaning: a barge horse on the towpath is something that tows
second meaning: completes the phrase for a dependable supporter

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer two ways: one who pulls a barge, and the tall building of 'a ___ of strength'.
explanation.definitionFit: A barge horse is a tugger along the bank, and a reliable person is called a tower of strength.

clue.text: Save up four, see, like Jack Dawkins

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from the bottom

blocks.note: taken as written
Roman numeral four
a see is a bishop's diocese; Ely is one

explanation.surface: Instructions for hoarding four of something, followed by a comparison to a Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dawkins is the Artful Dodger in Oliver Twist; a dodger behaves this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodging means avoiding, so acting like the Dodger is behaving in a slippery, avoiding manner.

clue.text: Advantage of an oriental drink

blocks.note: first meaning: benefit, as in 'for the ___ of'
second meaning: Japanese rice wine

explanation.walkthrough: The same spelling serves an English word for benefit and a Japanese drink.
explanation.definitionFit: 'For the sake of' means for the benefit of, and sake is also rice wine from Japan.

clue.text: Favourite antonym

blocks.note: surface reading: a best-loved word of opposite meaning
setter's reading: the opposite of the favourite in a race

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a beloved opposite; it is the opposite of a race favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: In betting, the runner least expected to win contrasts with the one most backed.

clue.text: Lyric composer

blocks.note: surface reading: a writer of song words
setter's reading: a joyful lyric song, here called a composer in loose cryptic style

explanation.walkthrough: A carol is a joyful song; the parse of 'composer' is loose, perhaps the verb sense of someone who sings it.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol is a lyrical song of joy, especially a Christmas hymn.

clue.text: Arctic footwear repaired so she won

indicators.note: something repaired is put back together differently, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: She mended her polar boots and so came first in the race.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowshoe is a broad frame strapped to a boot for walking on deep snow.

clue.text: An ocean greyhound, captain?

blocks.note: first meaning: a dog of the sea, read literally
second meaning: an old experienced sailor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ocean greyhound' suggests a fast liner; taken literally it is a dog at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasoned mariner is called an old salt, and a dog of the ocean puns on that.

clue.text: Mater knew the difference of course

indicators.note: making a difference to the words changes their order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: Mother could, naturally, tell things apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as 'naturally'; here 'course' alone is the definition, a racecourse. NEWMARKET is the famous English racecourse in Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: Newmarket is a racecourse, the home of British flat racing.

clue.text: Princess an artist born

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist
née is used before a woman's maiden name, meaning born

explanation.surface: A royal lady who was born with a painter's gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'an' is only joining the parts; it supplies no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranee is a Hindu queen or princess, the wife of a rajah.

clue.text: Six-footer has female body in queer gear

indicators.note: queer in its old sense of odd or strange marks letters set out in a strange order
one group of letters sits inside the other

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, a body of women
taken as written

explanation.surface: A very tall man shows off a woman's figure in strange clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it is an insect, which has six legs. The WI (Women's Institute) is a British women's organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: An earwig is an insect, and every insect walks on six legs.

clue.text: Head so comfortably placed in retirement

definitions.text: Head so comfortably placed in retirement

blocks.clueFragment: Head so comfortably placed in retirement
blocks.note: surface reading: a leader settled nicely into life after work
setter's reading: retiring is going to bed, where the head is laid on something soft

explanation.surface: A former chief settled nicely into a pensioned life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' seems to be a headmaster; it is the body part, and 'retirement' is bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: A head laid on a cushion in bed has been rested that way, the past participle of the verb.

clue.text: Orange overcoat?

blocks.note: first meaning: the Northern Irish province, stronghold of the Protestant Orange Order
second meaning: a long heavy loose coat with a cape

explanation.walkthrough: 'Orange' looks like the fruit or colour; it stands for the Orange Order, whose heartland is the province of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The province is loyalist Orange country, and the same name is given to a heavy belted greatcoat first made in Belfast.

clue.text: They are to beer what ale is to cakes

definitions.text: They are to beer what ale is to cakes

blocks.note: surface reading: an analogy about brewing ingredients
setter's reading: 'cakes and ale' and 'beer and ___' are both phrases for idle pleasure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cakes and ale' and 'beer and skittles' are both stock phrases for easy enjoyment; skittles is the pub game of ninepins.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'life is not all beer and skittles' pairs the drink with this pub game.

clue.text: "Thorny-s, be not seen" (M. N. Dream)

blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a word missing before the s
setter's reading: the fairies' lullaby in A Midsummer Night's Dream lists the spiny creatures banished from Titania's bower

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in Shakespeare's line 'Thorny ___s, be not seen' from the fairies' song in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The song warns off a prickly little mammal, whose spines make it the thorny creature of the line.

clue.text: A writer or Longfellow's mighty man?

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
'The smith, a mighty man is he', from The Village Blacksmith

explanation.surface: Is the person an author, or the hero of a famous poem?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a conjunction but is heraldry's gold. Oliver Goldsmith wrote The Vicar of Wakefield.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Goldsmith was an Irish novelist, playwright and poet.

clue.text: Plant vandal, given all clear to go by air

blocks.note: a green light signals that all is clear
travelling by air is flying

explanation.surface: A saboteur at a factory is cleared to fly away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory; it is a garden plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenfly are aphids, sap-sucking insects that damage garden plants.

clue.text: Origin of Kipling's Lady and the Tramp

definitions.text: Origin of Kipling's Lady and the Tramp

blocks.note: surface reading: two women from Kipling's poem The Ladies, a colonel's lady and a vagrant girl
setter's reading: a lady can be a fine passenger vessel and a tramp a cargo steamer, both built in the same place

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling wrote that 'the Colonel's Lady an' Judy O'Grady are sisters under their skins'; here lady and tramp are vessels, and their common origin is where they are built.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships, liners and tramp steamers alike, are built and launched at a yard on the waterfront.

clue.text: Start journey to South east? Swell!

blocks.note: compass abbreviation
a swell is a dandy, a toff

explanation.surface: Heading off to the south-east coast, a traveller exclaims how great it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell!' reads as an exclamation of delight; it is the noun, a toff, British slang for a smart upper-class man.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off is to begin a trip, depart.

clue.text: One of our coats of arms'? On the contrary

definitions.text: One of our coats of arms'? On the contrary

blocks.clueFragment: One of our coats of arms'?
blocks.note: surface reading: a heraldic shield
setter's reading: swap the words to get one of our arms' coats, the part of a garment that covers an arm

explanation.walkthrough: Turning the phrase round gives 'one of our arms' coats': the cloth an arm wears.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeve is the part of a coat that covers each arm, so it clothes the limb.

clue.text: State delivery service

blocks.note: first meaning: to put into words
second meaning: fast dispatch of post or parcels

explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation or postal state; it is the verb meaning to say.
explanation.definitionFit: To express an idea is to put it into words, and express post is a rapid mailing service.

clue.text: Altogether picturesque, this lady

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who is entirely pretty as a picture
setter's reading: a fairground lady covered all over in inked pictures

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picturesque' means full of pictures, and 'altogether' hints at the fairground lady stripped to show them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattooed lady was a sideshow act whose whole skin was decorated with inked designs.

clue.text: Comparatively like these 'ounds on the scent?

definitions.text: Comparatively like these 'ounds on the scent?

blocks.note: surface reading: hounds, with the dropped h of a cockney or hunting voice
setter's reading: hounds on the scent are hot on it, so this asks for the comparative of hot, said without its h

explanation.walkthrough: Hounds hot on a scent are, comparatively, more hot; say that comparative without its h, as the clue's 'ounds does, and you get the animal these hounds hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Otterhounds are the breed bred to hunt this river mammal, so 'these hounds' are its pursuers.

clue.text: State of Mary by sweet Afton

definitions.text: State of Mary by sweet Afton

blocks.note: surface reading: perhaps a US state, Maryland
setter's reading: Burns's song Sweet Afton asks the river to flow gently because Mary is sleeping by its stream

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns: 'Flow gently, sweet Afton... my Mary's asleep by thy murmuring stream.' 'State' is her condition, not a territory.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song Mary is sleeping beside the river, so her condition is slumber.

clue.text: Napoleon was one retired on his island

definitions.text: Napoleon was one retired on his island

blocks.note: surface reading: an emperor, as famous people are
setter's reading: he was banished to Elba and then St Helena

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' suggests a peaceful pension; his island years were enforced banishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was banished from France to islands, making him a person expelled from home.

clue.text: Sort of runner not allowed on the mountain-side

indicators.note: 'not allowed' asks for the letters meaning allowed to be left out

blocks.note: the scarlet runner is a climbing bean
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: An athlete of some kind is banned from racing on the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' looks like an athlete; it is the scarlet runner bean.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a steep rocky cliff or bare face on a hillside.

clue.text: Like greyhounds from the "slips?'".'

blocks.note: surface reading: comparing something to racing dogs
setter's reading: dogs let loose from the slips, the leashes that hold them, run very swiftly

explanation.walkthrough: Slips are the leashes greyhounds strain at before release; the printed punctuation after it is garbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet is an adjective for swift, as greyhounds are when released.

clue.text: Copy of bills I'm entering in the dossier

indicators.note: things that enter go inside something else

blocks.note: accounts, abbreviated A/Cs
taken as written
a dossier is a file of papers

explanation.surface: A clerk slips duplicate invoices into a folder.
explanation.walkthrough: A bill is an account, abbreviated AC in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A facsimile is an exact reproduction, a duplicate of a document.

clue.text: Revolutionary aids to Buddhist devotions

blocks.note: surface reading: radical, overthrowing the old order
setter's reading: devotional devices that work by turning round and round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests political upheaval; it means spinning.
explanation.definitionFit: Tibetan Buddhists spin cylinders inscribed with prayers, each turn counting as a recitation.
